source: Nersessian (2007) Mental Modeling in Conceptual Change (Handbook of Conceptual Change)
finding: Defines cognitive-historical analysis. It pairs detailed case studies of concept change with study of the basic human cognition the methods grow out of. Basis is a naturalist epistemology: scientists' methods grow out of everyday abilities (mental modeling, analogy, abstraction, visualisation, simulative imagining) and were bootstrapped by reflective method building.
numbers: No counts. Method statement, with one sofa-through-doorway example of mental modeling.
quote: the problem-solving practices of scientists arise out of and are constrained by basic cognitive capacities
limits: A framework and argument, not a tested hypothesis. Rests on case selection by the author. No base rates of how often each operator precedes a breakthrough.
agent_relevance: Licenses using lab findings on ordinary reasoning as a guide to the agent's operators. But it gives no evidence for WHEN in a problem an operator is applied, which our S6 placement needs.

source: Nersessian (2007) Mental Modeling in Conceptual Change (Handbook of Conceptual Change) - Maxwell case
finding: Maxwell chose continuum mechanics as the analogy source, then narrowed it to elastic fluids using constraints from the electromagnetic target (rotation giving vortices; geometry giving lines of force). The result was a hybrid model with its own emergent constraints. Simulating the vortex model in imagination exposed friction between touching vortices. Fixing that led to a second source (machine mechanics), the idle wheel, and a second hybrid model.
numbers: Sequence: vortex model, then friction constraint, then idle wheel (2 hybrid models). Source domains used: 2 (elastic fluids, machine mechanics).
quote: Following out the problem of accommodating the model constraint of friction led him to another source domain, machine mechanics
limits: Nersessian says it is 'likely' Maxwell found the friction constraint by imaginative simulation. This is inference from the 1861-62 text, not a record of his thinking. Other historians interpret the episode differently.
agent_relevance: Direct template: build a model from constraints of both source and target, run it mentally, let the failure (impasse) point to the next source. This matches O6 (model) feeding O7 (analogy) at an impasse.

source: Nersessian (2007) Mental Modeling in Conceptual Change (Handbook of Conceptual Change) - generic abstraction
finding: Generic abstraction is the step that turned the idle-wheel/vortex mechanism into a field. Maxwell abstracted from the specific mechanism to what it shares with the class of systems where one part passes motion to another continuously. That gave continuous-action transmission, i.e. the field concept. Other abstraction types named: idealisation, limiting case.
numbers: 3 abstraction types named; reasoning at the level of a model class rather than one model.
quote: reasoning about a specific spring or reasoning about it as representative of the class of simple harmonic oscillators
limits: Descriptive. No test of whether the abstraction step can be prompted or measured.
agent_relevance: An explicit operator candidate: after a model works, restate it with the specifics dropped (keep the relational dynamics) and reason about the class. Check against schema section 4b before adding.

source: Nersessian (2007) Mental Modeling in Conceptual Change (Handbook of Conceptual Change) - mental simulation evidence
finding: Summarises lab work behind simulative reasoning: mental rotation latencies scale with degrees of rotation; people simulate moving around a wall, not through it; in pulley and gear studies (Hegarty, Schwartz) people animate in causal order, piecemeal, not all at once; realistic gears give better performance than schematic circles; mental animation can give correct inferences when the person cannot describe them.
numbers: Latency grows with rotation angle (Shepard, Cooper, Kosslyn). Gear response time proportional to rotation angle. Participants trained in rules switch to rules and answer faster.
limits: Second-hand summary of other studies. Few studies with scientists (Clement, Trafton). Expertise shifts people from simulation to rules.
agent_relevance: Supports step-wise simulation traces (one causal step at a time) and warns that a known rule beats simulation. Fits G10: use the executed result, not the narrated reasoning.

source: Gentner, Brem, Ferguson, Wolff, Markman, Forbus (1997) Analogy and creativity in the works of Johannes Kepler
finding: A cognitive-historical study of Kepler using structure-mapping (SME). They coded Kepler's beliefs about light (5 beliefs) and the motive power (vis motrix) and ran SME. It highlighted the shared structure (emanation reaches planet), projected inferences (power travels from sun, volume times concentration constant, speed falls with distance, detectable only on arrival), and showed where the mapping failed.
numbers: Light knowledge coded as 5 beliefs. SME produced 4 candidate inferences. Kepler replaced Copernicus's at least 34 circles with 6 ellipses. Mars orbit mismatch 8 minutes of arc forced him to drop circles. Kepler wrote he repeated one calculation 'at least seventy times'.
quote: SME makes spontaneous inferences from its comparison process, unlike many other models of analogy
limits: Authors say they simulate 'some, though not all' of his mappings. Knowledge representations were hand-coded by the authors. Kepler's texts may be partly rhetoric; authors argue the intensity and repeated returns to the analogy show real use.
agent_relevance: Shows analogy as a structured process: align, project candidate inferences, test each. The test step is where our code checks (G2, G3) belong, since SME projects inferences without judging validity.

source: Gentner et al. (1997) Kepler - four analogical processes of conceptual change
finding: Four analogical subprocesses change a concept: highlighting (what aligns), projection (candidate inferences), re-representation (rewrite either side to improve the match), restructuring. Kepler re-represented 'travel is instantaneous but action takes time': light needs only touch a surface, the force must act on the planet's body and so takes time. This let the first part of the inference be accepted and only the second rejected.
numbers: 4 processes. 1 worked re-representation (light is instantaneous, force acts in time).
quote: Kepler gains a partial identity by decomposing and re-representing a previously problematic correspondence
limits: Restructuring from one base alone can mislead; the paper cites Faraday's iron-filings analogy that gave an over-concrete field model. Most restructuring likely needs several analogies applied in turn.
agent_relevance: Operator spec for O7: do not accept or reject an analogy whole. Split the failing inference and re-represent the mismatched relation. Also a warning: a single analogy can over-concretise.

source: Gentner et al. (1997) Kepler - alignable differences and inverse law
finding: After alignment, connected differences become salient. Kepler used one to argue light and motive power are not the same thing: an eclipse blocks light but does not stop planetary motion. He also knew light falls as inverse square, yet needed a simple inverse law for the force, so he argued the force spreads only in a plane, not a sphere.
numbers: Light intensity inverse square; Kepler's force simple inverse (1/r) by the plane argument. 1 difference used to separate the domains.
limits: Kepler's dynamics was Aristotelian (force causes velocity). The law he reached for the force was wrong in Newtonian terms, so a careful analogy process still gave a wrong model.
agent_relevance: An analogy can yield a confident wrong model; keep a G3 check against data not used to build the analogy. Listing aligned differences is a cheap, checkable step.

source: Gentner et al. (1997) Kepler - evidence analogy was used, not just rhetoric
finding: The authors argue Kepler's analogies drove his thinking: he published failures and dead ends, left his 1596 book intact in 1621 with notes, put effort into the source domains (read Gilbert's De Magnete; wrote his own optics treatise), and returned to the same analogies across books.
numbers: 25 years between Mysterium Cosmographicum (1596) and the 1621 second edition. At least 2 major analogies (light, magnetism) plus a balance scale.
limits: Cannot be settled; the authors say there is no way to decide it definitively. Published texts are filtered.
agent_relevance: Method point: historical texts are weak evidence of process. Weight notebook-level and trace-level evidence higher than published narratives.

source: Nersessian and Chandrasekharan (2009) Hybrid analogies in conceptual innovation in science (Cognitive Systems Research 10:3)
finding: An ethnographic plus cognitive-historical case in a neural-engineering lab. Researchers made a physical model (a dish of living neurons) and a computational model of it. The computational model, built with constraints from the dish, the neuroscience literature and engineering, was the hybrid that led to a reconceptualisation of neural 'bursts' over about one year.
numbers: Case spans about 1 year; 2 linked analogical models (in vitro, in silico). Bootstrapping: constraints from target and from sources are 'straps', hybrid models are 'strap crossings'.
quote: analogy is a mechanism of conceptual innovation
limits: One lab, one case. Qualitative coding, no inter-rater numbers in the text read. Results argued, not tested.
agent_relevance: Evidence that analogy in practice is iterated model-building with several constraint sources, not a one-shot source-to-target transfer. Supports a loop of build, run, revise rather than single analogy retrieval.

source: Nersessian (2009) How do engineering scientists think? Topics in Cognitive Science 1:730-757
finding: Defines cognitive-historical analysis in use: examine historical records to understand cognition, not to write a history. Combined with cognitive ethnography of two biomedical engineering labs (tissue engineering Lab A, neural engineering Lab D). Argues reasoning is done by a researcher-plus-artifact system (distributed model-based cognition).
numbers: 148 interviews and 40 research meetings fully transcribed; over 800 hours of field observation; 5-year study, 2 years intensive per lab. Also lab notebooks, grant and dissertation proposals, e-mails.
quote: cognitive-historical analysis examines historical records with the objective of understanding cognition, rather than constructing an historical account per se
limits: Two labs only. Video of lab work was not feasible. Interpretive findings, no control condition.
agent_relevance: For an LLM agent, the artifact does part of the reasoning: the simulator, code runner and tests are part of the thinking system, which supports code-checked steps (G1 to G3) over text-only reasoning.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia: Scientific Discovery (section 9 on Nersessian, Dunbar, Darden)
finding: Neutral summary. Nersessian names three forms of model-based reasoning: analogical, visual, simulative (thought experiments). Conceptual innovation comes from new concepts that abstract and integrate source and target. Dunbar's in vivo studies show analogy central to lab practice; fixing experimental problems draws on close domains, new concepts draw on less similar ones. Darden: mechanisms found by schema instantiation (protein synthesis). BACON simulates Kepler's third law.
numbers: 3 model-based forms. Dunbar: near sources for fixes, far sources for new concepts.
limits: Entry does not use the phrase cognitive-historical. Maxwell and Faraday not covered there. Only first 100000 characters read.
agent_relevance: Gives a distance rule to test: near-domain analogies for repair at S5, far-domain for new representations at S6.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia: Models in science (section 3, Nersessian 2010; Hesse; Bartha)
finding: Cites Nersessian: model-based reasoning means inferences made by creating, manipulating, adapting and evaluating models. Hesse's neutral analogies (features not yet known to hold) suggest new hypotheses. Bartha (2010) argues analogical models cannot be confirmatory in a Bayesian sense; Hesse (1974) argues they can for material analogies.
numbers: No numbers. Debate: analogy as confirmation, yes (Hesse 1974) vs no (Bartha 2010).
limits: Philosophical dispute unresolved. Only first 100000 of 135499 characters read.
agent_relevance: Analogy generates hypotheses but should not count as proof. Matches G3 and G4.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) beat UCLA undergraduates on digit-matrix problems (generative OR 1.88, p=0.005; multiple choice OR 6.27, p=2.3e-8), on letter-string analogies overall (OR 1.76, p=6.3e-5, driven by zero-generalisation items), and matched or beat humans on verbal analogy sets and SAT analogies. It lost to humans on story analogies.
numbers: Matrices N=40 humans; letter-string N=57; verbal analogy N=57; story analogy N=54. Story analogy: humans better (OR 0.37, p=0.0003), 15 of 54 humans right on every trial. Far story analogies: GPT-3 not above chance (p=0.065). Radiation problem: with distractor stories GPT-3 lost the convergence solution, regained it when told to consider the earlier stories.
limits: Students are one human sample. Training-data overlap not ruled out here; see the counterfactual replication. GPT-4 said to do better on stories in an initial check only.
agent_relevance: The distractor result matches Gick and Holyoak: models find the analogy when told to look, and fail to retrieve it spontaneously. So O7 needs an explicit 'look for a relevant earlier case' prompt triggered by a signal.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Re-tested the Webb letter-string task with permuted alphabets and non-letter symbols. Humans stayed high. GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 dropped sharply on counterfactual versions. Error types differ: humans often used a different but sensible rule, GPT models more often gave wrong or incorrect-rule answers.
numbers: Share of errors that used an alternate rule: GPT-3 5.81%, GPT-4 22.00%, humans 38.59%. Incorrect-rule errors: GPT-3 and GPT-4 over 30%, humans about 15%. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 no better than GPT-3 on default items; GPT-3.5 worse. Human sample about 46 (their data) vs 57 (Webb).
limits: Partial failed replication of generality. Chat tuning may have hurt. Prompt used the Hodel and West alphabet-listing format. Per-condition accuracies are in figures and were not read as numbers.
agent_relevance: Do not trust analogy ability shown on familiar formats. Test O7 on altered surface forms (G3 mutated input).

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Benchmark of system analogies between narratives with near and far analogies and distractors. Models did reasonably when the analogy was near, but far analogies (little surface overlap) were below chance. Humans did well on both.
numbers: Telling analogies from distractors: models 57% vs humans 96% (chance 50%). Near analogies: humans 97.9%, models 75.0%. Far analogies: humans 94.1%, models 39.6% (below random). A plain SBERT similarity baseline reached 77.9% in the near setting. GPT-4 near humans on near analogies, below random on far.
limits: Table layout garbled in extraction; figures here come from the paper's prose. Zero-shot setting, models of the 2023 era.
agent_relevance: LLMs retrieve by surface similarity. Far-domain analogy, the kind Nersessian and Dunbar link to new concepts, is the weak spot. Do not rely on model-driven far retrieval without a structural check.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR 2024)
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes relevant past problems (and, for hard tasks, high-level knowledge) before solving. It beat 0-shot CoT and was close to hand-written few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench tasks.
numbers: K=5 self-generated exemplars on GSM8K, K=3 on MATH and BIG-Bench; Codeforces uses knowledge plus 3 exemplars. Codeforces: GPT-3.5-turbo with the method reached 15% Acc@1 vs GPT-4 3-shot CoT 16%. Generated exemplars beat retrieved ones only with larger models.
limits: For small or weak models retrieved exemplars did better, and generation can yield invalid exemplars. Per-cell tables were garbled in extraction and are not quoted.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for a cheap O7: generate your own related solved cases first. But G2 and G3 still apply because self-generated exemplars are unchecked.

source: Liu et al. (2022) Mind's Eye: grounded language model reasoning through simulation
finding: Uses a physics engine (MuJoCo) to simulate the question and feeds the result to the LM, an automated form of simulative modeling. Large gains on 39 physics-alignment tasks.
numbers: Average absolute gain 27.9% zero-shot, 46.0% few-shot. GPT-3 175B baseline 24% zero-shot, 38.2% few-shot. GPT-3 1.3B with Mind's Eye 29.8% vs vanilla 175B at 29%. One subtask: 46.7% to 84.2% with Mind's Eye, vs 36.4% to 38.2% with vanilla few-shot.
limits: Needs a simulator and a text-to-simulation translator; conversion error costs 3.6 to 4.7 points. Physics only. Older GPT-3 models.
agent_relevance: Best support for O6 as an executable model: run the model in code and read the output, not narrated mental simulation (G10).

source: Wu et al. (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought elicits spatial reasoning
finding: Asking the model to draw its intermediate state as text grids helped on navigation and tiling tasks and beat GPT-4V CoT. It did not help where a rule exists.
numbers: Boundary case: on ring navigation GPT-4 CoT beat VoT 52.5% vs 49.5% (200 items, ring size 12), because the task reduces to modular arithmetic. Main-table values garbled in extraction and not quoted.
limits: Gains depend on the task; weaker LLMs gained less; incorrect visualisations were common.
agent_relevance: Imagery-style traces help only where state tracking is the bottleneck. Add a gate: skip when a calculation rule exists (G1, G11).

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SR: scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Treats equations as programs; the LLM proposes skeletons from domain knowledge, a fitter sets parameters, evolutionary search iterates. Beat symbolic regression baselines, most in out-of-domain tests. Ablations show domain-prior text, programs and iteration all matter.
numbers: 2.5K iterations vs 2M+ for baselines. E. coli growth OOD NMSE about 0.0037 vs baselines above 1. Ablations on Oscillation 2: no iterative refinement NMSE 1.01e-1 in-domain and 1.81e-1 OOD; no skeleton+optimizer 3.78e-1 and 3.75e-1.
limits: Four benchmarks built to limit recitation; GPT-3.5 and Mixtral backbones; not real historical discoveries.
agent_relevance: A model (equation program) built from prior knowledge and refined against data fits the cognitive-historical pattern. Supports code-based checks and domain-prior text in the prompt.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji, Hope (2024) SciMON: scientific inspiration machines optimized for novelty
finding: Retrieves 'inspirations' (near and far literature) and iteratively revises ideas against prior work to raise novelty. GPT-4 alone gave ideas with low technical depth and novelty.
numbers: Iterative novelty boosting: first iteration gained novelty on 46.7% to 55.6% of treated ideas (best variant 55.6%); second iteration gained for 57.8% of those continued. Versus the real paper's idea, ground truth judged higher in technical level and novelty in 85% of comparisons. Study I: six NLP experts, 50 instances.
limits: Small human study; novelty judged by humans reading abstracts, not by running ideas (G8). Ideas get longer after iterations, a length confound.
agent_relevance: Retrieving inspirations is a form of cross-domain analogy, but the gain is novelty, not correctness; G8 says test by running.

source: Nersessian and Chandrasekharan (2009) Hybrid analogies - what current analogy theories miss
finding: Argues standard analogy models (one ready-made source mapped to a target) do not cover cases where scientists build an intermediate hybrid model carrying constraints of both source and target, then reason with the hybrid. They cite historical studies (Nersessian 1984, 1992; Spranzi 2005) and protocol studies (Clement 1989) that show the same hybrid construction.
numbers: 3 independent study types cited as showing hybrid construction: historical, protocol, ethnographic.
limits: Authors are partisan for their own framework; no head-to-head test against SME or ACME.
agent_relevance: Suggests our O7 should build and iterate an intermediate model rather than map one retrieved source onto the problem.

source: Nersessian (2008) Creating Scientific Concepts (MIT Press)
finding: Book-length statement: model-based reasoning (analogical, imagistic, simulative) is a means of generating new concepts, with Maxwell's 1861-62 'On Physical Lines of Force' as the main case and a think-aloud protocol of a scientist (S2, spring) as a second.
numbers: Not available.
limits: Not opened; only publisher blurbs and search summaries seen. Check chapters before citing details.
agent_relevance: Primary source to read next.

source: Maxwell (1861-62) On Physical Lines of Force
finding: Primary text for the vortex and idle-wheel model discussed in Nersessian. Not read this session.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Details taken only from Nersessian's secondary account.
agent_relevance: Source to verify the sequence vortex, friction, idle wheel.

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific Discovery; BACON (as reported in SEP)
finding: BACON and KEKADA search problem spaces with heuristics to find regularities; BACON simulates Kepler's third law. Reported second-hand via SEP, original not opened.
numbers: Not available.
limits: Data-driven search; no analogy or model construction.
agent_relevance: Contrasts with the model-building view: data-fit search finds laws, model building finds concepts.

source: Dunbar (1995, 1997, 2001) in vivo studies of molecular biology labs (as reported in SEP)
finding: In vivo lab study: analogy central to practice; near-domain analogies for experimental problems, less similar domains for new concepts. Second-hand through SEP only.
numbers: Not available.
limits: Not opened. Belongs to the laboratory-notebook subfield; do not duplicate.
agent_relevance: Cross-link to subfield 02.
